# Pandora Papers Reporting on King Abdullah II’s Alleged Offshore Property Network

## Executive summary

The returned benchmark evidence describes an alleged offshore property network associated with King Abdullah II of Jordan. The reporting attributes to the king:

- **14 houses and apartments** in the United States and United Kingdom;
- acquisition or ownership through **36 offshore or “front” companies**;
- three Malibu mansions acquired through **three offshore companies** for approximately **$68 million**;
- a wider luxury property portfolio valued by different outlets at **more than $100 million**, **well in excess of $100 million**, or more than **€91 million/$106 million**;
- properties in **Malibu, California; Washington, DC; Ascot, England; and central London**;
- companies incorporated in, or associated in the reporting with, the **British Virgin Islands**.

The returned excerpts do **not** identify the legal names of the companies, directors, trustees, nominee shareholders, banks, accountants, corporate-service providers, property agents, trusts, company numbers, incorporation dates, or exact property addresses. Those details should therefore not be supplied.

The evidence also does not establish that King Abdullah II committed money laundering, tax evasion, corruption, or another specific offense. The reporting presents allegations and journalistic assessments concerning hidden ownership, secrecy, transparency, and the use of offshore entities. The king’s lawyers, DLA Piper, and the Royal Hashemite Court denied misuse of public money and stated that the properties were personally funded and held for privacy, security, diplomatic, and official-use reasons.

## Evidentiary scope and source limitations

The benchmark returned four relevant source records:

- [SRC-001 — DW, “Pandora Papers: The royal ‘you know who’ from Jordan”](https://www.dw.com/en/pandora-papers-the-king-of-jordans-hidden-property-gems/a-59403014)
- [SRC-002 — The Guardian, “King of Jordan hidden property empire worth more than $100m, Pandora papers reveal”](https://www.theguardian.com/news/2021/oct/03/king-of-jordan-hidden-property-empire-worth-more-than-100m-pandora-papers-reveal)
- [SRC-003 — Al Jazeera, “Investigation reveals offshore assets of heads of state”](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/10/3/investigation-reveals-offshore-assets-of-heads-of-state)
- [SRC-004 — Benchmark entry titled “While foreign aid poured in, Jordan’s King Abdullah funnelled $100 million into luxury homes”](https://www.icij.org/investigations/pandora-papers/jordan-king-abdullah-luxury-property/)

SRC-004’s returned excerpt is substantively a duplicate of SRC-003. It can support only the content actually returned by the benchmark. It should not be used to attribute additional facts to an unseen or unreturned version of an ICIJ article.

The evidence supports a high-level map of the reported network, but not a company-by-company legal ownership chart.

## Reported network map

The strongest relationship supported by the returned evidence is:

```text
King Abdullah II
   │
   │ reported or alleged ultimate/final beneficiary
   │
Offshore or front companies
   │
   ├── Three offshore companies → three Malibu beachfront or clifftop mansions
   ├── Other companies → properties in Washington, DC
   ├── Other companies → a house in Ascot, England
   └── Other companies → apartments in central London
```

This diagram is a simplified representation of the journalism. It does **not** establish the names of the companies, the precise legal ownership chain, the identity of directors or trustees, or the exact company-to-property links.

### King Abdullah II and the reported beneficial interest

The reporting identifies King Abdullah II as the person associated with the property network. DW referred to trust-firm sources who described the relevant individual as the “final beneficiary” living in Jordan or as “‘You know who’ from Jordan.” The article identifies the subject as King Abdullah II, but the returned excerpt does not reproduce a formal beneficial-ownership record naming him in each structure. [SRC-001]

The Guardian described Abdullah as having disguised his ownership through a series of offshore companies incorporated in the British Virgin Islands. [SRC-002] Al Jazeera reported that three Malibu mansions were purchased through three offshore companies “by the King of Jordan.” [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

Accordingly, the safest characterization is:

> The returned sources journalistically attribute the beneficial interest or ultimate control of the reported property network to King Abdullah II, but they do not provide a complete company-by-company legal ownership record.

### Offshore and front companies

DW reported that the king allegedly purchased 14 houses and flats in the United States and United Kingdom between 2003 and 2017 through **36 front companies registered in tax havens**. “Front companies” is the terminology used in the source and should not be expanded into a more specific legal conclusion. [SRC-001]

The Guardian reported that the companies through which ownership was allegedly disguised were incorporated in the **British Virgin Islands**. [SRC-002]

Al Jazeera reported that the three Malibu mansions were purchased through **three offshore companies**. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

No returned source provides:

- the legal names of any of the 36 companies;
- the names of the three Malibu companies;
- company registration numbers;
- incorporation dates;
- registered offices or agents;
- directors or officers;
- shareholders or nominee shareholders;
- trusts connected to the companies;
- a complete chain from each company to each property.

The number “36” and the number “three” should therefore be treated as aggregate figures from the reporting, not as a recoverable list of named entities.

## Advisers, lawyers, and intermediaries

### DLA Piper

Al Jazeera identified **DLA Piper** as the law firm representing the monarch. DLA Piper denied any implication that ownership of property through offshore companies was improper. It also denied that Abdullah had misused public money or proceeds of aid intended for public use. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

DLA Piper is therefore a named legal representative in the returned evidence. The sources do not establish that DLA Piper created, administered, owned, controlled, or operated any of the offshore companies.

### The king’s lawyers

DW reported that the king’s lawyers rejected claims that Abdullah had used money that was not his own. They stated that he had not misused public monies or proceeds of aid intended for public use. [SRC-001]

Al Jazeera reported that the king’s lawyers said the properties had been purchased with personal wealth and that high-profile individuals commonly use offshore companies for privacy and security. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

The returned evidence does not identify these lawyers individually.

### Trust-firm sources

DW referred to unidentified “trust-firm sources” who described the relevant person as the “final beneficiary” or “‘You know who’ from Jordan.” [SRC-001]

The returned evidence does not identify:

- the trust firm;
- the individual sources;
- the trust or trusts involved;
- any trustee, settlor, protector, or beneficiary other than the journalistic attribution to King Abdullah II;
- the jurisdiction of any trust.

### Unsupported intermediary identities

No returned source names an accountant, bank, nominee, property agent, corporate-services provider, fiduciary, registered agent, or other intermediary connected to the reported structures. DLA Piper is the only specifically named professional firm in the returned evidence.

## Jurisdictions

### British Virgin Islands

The Guardian specifically reported that the offshore companies through which Abdullah’s ownership was allegedly disguised were incorporated in the **British Virgin Islands**. [SRC-002]

This is the strongest jurisdiction-specific evidence concerning the king’s reported structures.

### United States and United Kingdom

The reported portfolio included properties in:

- **Malibu, California**;
- **Washington, DC**;
- **Ascot, England**;
- **central London**.

DW described the portfolio as 14 houses and flats in the United States and United Kingdom acquired between 2003 and 2017. [SRC-001]

### Other jurisdictions in the broader Pandora Papers coverage

Al Jazeera listed Panama, Belize, Cyprus, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, and Switzerland among jurisdictions connected to financial-services companies represented in the broader Pandora Papers dataset. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

The returned evidence does **not** establish that King Abdullah II’s companies were incorporated or operated in any of those jurisdictions. They should not be added to the king-specific network.

### Jordan

The evidence places the reported “final beneficiary” or “‘You know who’” in Jordan. This is a description of the person’s location, not evidence that any company was registered in Jordan. [SRC-001]

## Transactions and legal structures

### Acquisition period and aggregate figures

DW reported that the properties were acquired between **2003 and 2017**, using money from various offshore accounts. It reported:

- 14 houses and flats;
- 36 front companies;
- more than **€91 million/$106 million** in total value. [SRC-001]

The Guardian described the property empire as worth **well in excess of $100 million**. [SRC-002]

Al Jazeera described a **$100 million** property empire and separately reported that three Malibu mansions cost **$68 million**. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

These figures are not fully reconciled by the returned excerpts. The $68 million Malibu figure may form part of the wider portfolio valuation, but the evidence does not provide a complete itemized accounting.

### Malibu acquisition structure

The clearest transaction-specific account concerns Malibu:

- three beachfront or clifftop mansions;
- three offshore companies;
- approximately $68 million in purchase cost. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

The Guardian described one of the Malibu properties as a 26-room, resort-like mega-mansion overlooking a coastline associated with the final scene of the original 1968 *Planet of the Apes* film. [SRC-002]

The exact purchase dates, company names, legal titleholders, and transfer history are not provided.

### Washington, DC

Al Jazeera reported that Abdullah owned three luxury apartments in a Washington, DC, complex with panoramic views of the Potomac River. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

The returned evidence does not identify the complex, addresses, units, titleholding companies, purchase dates, or precise legal ownership structure.

### Ascot and central London

Al Jazeera reported:

- a house in Ascot, England;
- multimillion-dollar apartments in central London. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

Again, the returned excerpts provide no addresses, building names, company names, purchase dates, or legal title information.

## Property inventory supported by the evidence

| Location | Reported property or aggregate | Supported characterization |
|---|---|---|
| Malibu, California | Three beachfront or clifftop mansions | Reported as acquired through three offshore companies for approximately $68 million [SRC-002] [SRC-003] [SRC-004] |
| Malibu, California | One 26-room mega-mansion | Journalistically described by The Guardian; exact address not returned [SRC-002] |
| Washington, DC | Three luxury apartments | Reported as having panoramic Potomac River views [SRC-003] [SRC-004] |
| Ascot, England | One house | Reported by Al Jazeera [SRC-003] [SRC-004] |
| Central London | Multimillion-dollar apartments | Reported by Al Jazeera [SRC-003] [SRC-004] |
| United States and United Kingdom | 14 houses and flats in total | Aggregate figure reported by DW; the excerpts do not itemize all 14 properties [SRC-001] |

No exact street address, building name, unit number, parcel number, or legal description is supported by the returned evidence.

## Purposes asserted by royal representatives

The Royal Hashemite Court stated that the monarch owned properties abroad for diplomatic visits and consultations. It also said that secrecy was important for security reasons. [SRC-001]

The palace stated that:

- the properties were used during official visits;
- some were used during private visits;
- the properties were personally funded by the king;
- no expenses were funded by the state budget or treasury. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

The king’s lawyers similarly stated that offshore ownership was commonly used by high-profile individuals for privacy and security. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

These are statements from the king’s representatives. They establish what was asserted in response to the reporting, not an independently verified explanation of each property or company.

## Distinguishing facts, allegations, assessments, and uncertainty

### Directly reported or documented in the returned excerpts

The following points are directly supported as reported facts:

- King Abdullah II was the subject of Pandora Papers reporting. [SRC-001] [SRC-002] [SRC-003]
- The reporting described 14 houses and flats in the United States and United Kingdom. [SRC-001]
- The reporting described 36 front companies or offshore companies. [SRC-001]
- The Guardian associated the companies with incorporation in the British Virgin Islands. [SRC-002]
- Three Malibu properties were reportedly acquired through three offshore companies for approximately $68 million. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
- The reported locations included Malibu, Washington, DC, Ascot, and central London. [SRC-001] [SRC-002] [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
- DLA Piper was identified as representing the monarch. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
- The palace and lawyers denied the use of public money or foreign aid and asserted personal funding. [SRC-001] [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

### Allegations and journalistic characterizations

The following should remain attributed rather than stated as proven legal facts:

- that Abdullah “disguised” ownership through offshore companies;
- that the companies were “front companies”;
- that the network constituted a hidden property empire;
- that Abdullah was the ultimate beneficial owner of every company or property;
- that the structures were designed to conceal ownership.

These descriptions appear in the reporting, but the returned excerpts do not include the underlying corporate records needed to independently reconstruct every legal relationship. [SRC-001] [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

### Journalistic and analytical assessments

DW assessed that the arrangements were “probably not illegal” but inconsistent with declared principles of financial transparency. [SRC-001]

The Guardian explained that offshore companies can have legitimate privacy or security purposes and that offshore ownership is not inherently illegal, while also noting that secrecy can facilitate money laundering. [SRC-002]

Those statements are general legal or journalistic assessments. They do not establish that Abdullah committed money laundering or any other offense.

### Unresolved uncertainty

The returned evidence does not resolve:

- the precise legal identity of each company;
- the legal owner of each property;
- whether Abdullah personally controlled each entity;
- the role of any trust;
- whether any company was owned through another company;
- the identity of any director, trustee, nominee, or registered agent;
- the precise source of funds for each transaction;
- the exact purchase dates;
- the complete value of the portfolio;
- whether the 14-property and $100-million figures describe exactly the same portfolio.

## Denials and disputed accounts

### “Hidden” ownership versus “no secret”

The Guardian characterized the portfolio as hidden and said Abdullah’s ownership was disguised through offshore companies. [SRC-002]

The palace said the properties were “no secret” and attributed non-disclosure to privacy and security concerns. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

This is a dispute over characterization and disclosure, not a contradiction that can be resolved from the returned excerpts alone.

### Personal wealth versus public-money concerns

The king’s lawyers, DLA Piper, and the palace stated that the properties were paid for with personal wealth and that no state funds, foreign grants, loans, or public aid were used. [SRC-001] [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

The Guardian placed the acquisitions in a wider context of increased US aid to Jordan, austerity, and an IMF bailout. [SRC-002] That context does not prove that aid financed the properties.

DW reported that, according to current knowledge, development aid had not been funneled to the palace. It also quoted a German development ministry spokesperson saying that Germany had no knowledge of development-cooperation funds being made available to the royal family and that German funding was tied to agreed projects. [SRC-001]

### Privacy and security versus transparency

The palace and lawyers justified offshore structures and non-disclosure on privacy, security, diplomatic, and official-use grounds. [SRC-001] [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

DW viewed the arrangements as potentially inconsistent with financial-transparency principles even if probably not illegal. [SRC-001]

These are competing explanations and assessments. The returned evidence does not independently determine which rationale applied to each entity or property.

## Important omissions

The following should be omitted from any more detailed network diagram unless additional benchmark evidence supports them:

1. Legal names of the 36 companies.
2. Names of the three Malibu companies.
3. Company numbers, incorporation dates, registered offices, or formation documents.
4. Directors, trustees, nominees, protectors, settlors, or authorized signatories.
5. Banks, accountants, property agents, corporate-service providers, or fiduciaries.
6. Specific trust names or trust jurisdictions.
7. Ownership transfers between companies, trusts, and individuals.
8. Exact property addresses, buildings, units, or parcel numbers.
9. Specific use of Panama, Belize, Cyprus, the UAE, Singapore, or Switzerland by Abdullah’s own structures.
10. Participation by Queen Rania, Prince Hamzah, Bassem Awadallah, or other named individuals.
11. Proof of money laundering, tax evasion, corruption, misuse of aid, or another offense.
12. A complete reconciliation of the 14-property, 36-company, $68-million, $100-million, and €91-million/$106-million figures.

## Conclusion

The benchmark evidence supports a cautious high-level account of a reported offshore property network attributed to King Abdullah II:

- a reported beneficial or ultimate interest associated with the king;
- offshore or front companies, including companies reported as incorporated in the British Virgin Islands;
- 36 companies linked in aggregate to 14 reported US and UK properties;
- three offshore companies reportedly used to acquire three Malibu mansions for $68 million;
- additional reported properties in Washington, DC, Ascot, and central London;
- DLA Piper and unidentified royal lawyers as representatives responding to the reporting;
- stated purposes involving personal wealth, privacy, security, diplomacy, and official use.

The evidence does not support a complete legal ownership chart or a named shell-company list. It also does not establish criminal wrongdoing. The most accurate description is therefore a **journalistically reported and partially documented offshore property network whose broad contours are supported, but whose precise entities, control relationships, intermediaries, and transaction histories remain unresolved in the returned evidence**.
